title: Why does a naive `if (!alreadyProcessed(id)) { process(); markProcessed(id); }` dedup still double-process under concurrency or on crash, and what are the two fixes — make the dedup write atomic (`INSERT ... ` with a `UNIQUE(event_id)` constraint so only one consumer wins) and commit the business update and the dedup record in the SAME database transaction (so a crash after the update but before marking cannot cause reprocessing to re-apply it)?
shortTitle: Why does a naive `if (!alreadyProcessed(id)) { process(); markProcessed(id); }` dedup still double-process

s1_definition.profdef: The naive check-then-act dedup fails in two distinct ways. Under concurrency, two consumers both call `alreadyProcessed(id)`, both see false, and both process, because the gap between the check and the mark is a race window. On crash, a consumer processes the business change but crashes before `markProcessed(id)`, so on redelivery the id is still unmarked and the work is re-applied. The two fixes are to make the dedup write atomic with a unique constraint on the event id so only one consumer can win the insert, and to commit the business update and the dedup record in the same database transaction so a crash cannot separate them.
s1_definition.analogy: Two clerks at National Bank of India both glance at the logbook, both see the instruction number is not logged yet, and both credit Priya, because the glance and the pen-stroke were separate actions with a gap between them. Separately, one clerk credits Priya but faints before writing the number in the logbook, so when the instruction comes again it looks brand new and Priya is credited twice. The fix is a logbook that physically allows each number to be written only once so only one clerk wins, and doing the credit and the logbook entry as one inseparable action so fainting cannot split them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Naive dedup double-processes because the check and the mark are separate, racing under concurrency and losing the mark on crash, so you make the mark an atomic unique insert that only one consumer wins and commit it in the same transaction as the business change.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The naive check-then-act dedup fails in two distinct ways. Under concurrency, two consumers both call `alreadyProcessed(id)`, both see false, and both process, because the gap between the check and the mark is a race window. On crash, a consumer processes the business change but crashes before `markProcessed(id)`, so on redelivery the id is still unmarked and the work is re-applied. The two fixes are to make the dedup write atomic with a unique constraint on the event id so only one consumer can win the insert, and to commit the business update and the dedup record in the same database transaction so a crash cannot separate them.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two clerks at National Bank of India both glance at the logbook, both see the instruction number is not logged yet, and both credit Priya, because the glance and the pen-stroke were separate actions with a gap between them. Separately, one clerk credits Priya but faints before writing the number in the logbook, so when the instruction comes again it looks brand new and Priya is credited twice. The fix is a logbook that physically allows each number to be written only once so only one clerk wins, and doing the credit and the logbook entry as one inseparable action so fainting cannot split them.

**One line to remember:** Naive dedup double-processes because the check and the mark are separate, racing under concurrency and losing the mark on crash, so you make the mark an atomic unique insert that only one consumer wins and commit it in the same transaction as the business change.

sections.s2_technical:
Look closely at the naive code: `if (!alreadyProcessed(id)) { process(); markProcessed(id); }`. It has three separate operations, a read, a side effect, and a write, with no atomicity binding them, and both failure modes live in the gaps between them.

The concurrency failure is a classic check-then-act race. Two consumers in a consumer group, or the same message delivered to two instances, both execute `alreadyProcessed(id)` at nearly the same time. Because neither has marked the id yet, both reads return false. Both then proceed into `process()`, applying the business effect twice, and both call `markProcessed(id)` afterward. The read and the subsequent write are not a single atomic operation, so there is a window in which both consumers believe they are the first. No amount of ordering the three lines differently fixes this; the problem is that the decision and the claim are not atomic.

The crash failure is about the gap between `process()` and `markProcessed(id)`. Suppose a single consumer runs `process()`, which applies the business change, and then the process is killed before `markProcessed(id)` executes. The business effect is already applied, but the id was never marked. When the broker redelivers the message, because at-least-once delivery guarantees it will, the consumer runs `alreadyProcessed(id)`, sees false because the mark never happened, and re-applies the business change. Even if the two writes are in the right order, a crash between them re-applies the work.

The first fix makes the dedup write atomic so the claim itself decides the winner. Instead of reading then writing, you attempt a single atomic insert of the event id into a table with a unique constraint, `INSERT INTO inbox(event_id) VALUES(?)` where `event_id` is `UNIQUE`. The database guarantees only one insert of a given id can succeed; the concurrent second consumer's insert fails with a duplicate-key error. So you process only if your insert succeeded, and you treat the duplicate-key error as "someone else owns this event, skip". This collapses the check-then-act window into one atomic operation that the database arbitrates, which is the only reliable arbiter under concurrency.

The second fix binds the business update and the dedup record into one database transaction so a crash cannot separate them. You do `BEGIN; INSERT INTO inbox(event_id) ...; <business update>; COMMIT;`. Now there are only two possible outcomes: either the transaction commits, in which case both the mark and the business change are durably present together, or it does not commit, in which case neither is, and a redelivery can safely redo the whole thing. There is no state where the business change is applied but the id is unmarked, which is exactly the state that caused the crash double-processing. The two fixes are complementary: the unique constraint handles concurrency by picking one winner, and the single transaction handles crashes by making the mark and the effect atomic.

Senior nuances: the business update must be in the same transactional resource as the inbox for the single-transaction guarantee to hold, which is straightforward when both are in the same database but requires the transactional outbox or careful design when the side effect is external, like sending an email, since you cannot enlist an email in a database transaction. In that case you record intent in the transaction and perform the external effect idempotently afterward. Also, you acknowledge the message to the broker only after the transaction commits, so a crash before commit simply causes a safe redelivery. This pattern is the transactional inbox, the consumer-side mirror of the transactional outbox.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Two instances of a National Bank of India consumer both received the same `MoneyCredited` event, both checked the processed table and saw it absent, and both credited Priya. This is exactly the concurrency race, fixed by an atomic unique insert of the event id so only one instance wins.

Problem 2 — A consumer credited Priya then crashed before marking the event processed, and the redelivery credited her again. This is exactly the crash gap, fixed by committing the credit and the processed-record in one transaction.

Problem 3 — The team first tried just reordering the lines and it still double-processed, proving ordering is not the fix. This is exactly why atomicity, not ordering, is the real solution.

Our mini-project contrasts the naive and the fixed consumer. The code defines a `NaiveConsumer` with the racy check-then-act, a `SafeConsumer` using an atomic unique insert plus a single transaction, an `InboxStore` enforcing uniqueness, and a demo that runs concurrent duplicate deliveries and a crash scenario against both, showing the naive one double-credits and the safe one does not.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: event EVT-1 to the naive consumer delivered concurrently twice; EVT-2 to the safe consumer concurrently twice; EVT-3 to the safe consumer with a crash then a redelivery.

Step 1: Two threads deliver EVT-1 to the naive consumer at once. Both call `alreadyProcessed("EVT-1")` in the race window and both get false. Both credit Priya and both mark the id afterward, so Priya may end up at 350000 instead of 300000. The check and the mark were not atomic, so both believed they were first.

Step 2: Two threads deliver EVT-2 to the safe consumer at once. Both call `claimAtomically("EVT-2")`, but the unique insert allows only one to succeed; the loser gets false and skips. Only one credit happens, so Priya is correctly at 300000. The atomic claim decided the winner.

Step 3: The safe consumer processes EVT-3, crediting 10000 and recording the claim in the same transaction, which commits, and then a crash occurs before the broker acknowledgment.

Step 4: Because the claim and the credit committed together, the redelivery of EVT-3 finds the claim already present and skips the credit. Priya is credited exactly once despite the crash, because there was no state where the credit was applied but the id unmarked.

Step 5: The contrast is decisive: the naive consumer double-processes under concurrency, while the safe consumer, using an atomic unique claim and a single transaction, handles both concurrency and crash correctly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
I answer this by dissecting the naive code, because both bugs live in the gaps between its three unatomic operations: a read with alreadyProcessed, a side effect with process, and a write with markProcessed. The concurrency failure is a textbook check-then-act race. Two consumers, or the same message delivered to two instances, both call alreadyProcessed at nearly the same instant, both see false because neither has marked yet, and both proceed to process and then mark. The read and the later write are not one atomic operation, so there is a window where both believe they are first, and reordering the three lines cannot fix it because the decision and the claim are simply not atomic.

The crash failure is about the gap between process and markProcessed. A single consumer applies the business change in process, then is killed before markProcessed runs. The effect is already durable but the id was never marked, so when the broker redelivers, which at-least-once delivery guarantees, the consumer sees the id as unprocessed and re-applies the change. Even with the lines in the right order, a crash between them re-processes.

The two fixes attack the two root causes directly. First, I make the dedup write atomic by attempting a single insert of the event id into a table with a unique constraint rather than reading then writing. The database guarantees only one insert of a given id can succeed, so a concurrent second consumer's insert fails with a duplicate-key error, and I process only if my insert succeeded and skip on the duplicate-key error. That collapses the check-then-act window into one atomic operation that the database arbitrates, which is the only reliable arbiter under concurrency. Second, I commit the business update and the inbox record in the same database transaction, so the only outcomes are both durably present together or neither present, and there is never the dangerous state where the effect is applied but the id is unmarked, which is exactly what caused the crash double-processing. The two fixes are complementary: the unique constraint handles concurrency by picking one winner, and the single transaction handles crashes by making the mark and the effect inseparable.

On my project at National Bank of India we hit both. Two consumer instances double-credited Priya because both passed the naive check, and separately a consumer credited her then crashed before marking, and the redelivery credited her again. We fixed it with a transactional inbox: an atomic insert into an inbox table with a unique event id to pick the single winner, and the credit committed in the same transaction as that insert, with the message acknowledged to the broker only after the commit. The team had first tried just reordering the lines and it still double-processed, which taught everyone that the fix is atomicity, not ordering. The external-side-effect caveat I always add is that when the effect is something like an email that cannot join the database transaction, I record intent in the transaction and perform the external action idempotently afterward.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that naive check-then-act dedup double-processes because the check and the mark are separate, so it races under concurrency and loses the mark on crash, and I fix it by making the mark an atomic insert under a unique event-id constraint so only one consumer wins and by committing that mark in the same transaction as the business change so a crash can never leave the effect applied but unmarked.
